questions.q: If the vector sum of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$), the total angular momentum of the system relative to its center of mass is conserved over time.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between the net external force and the net external torque.
explanations: Incorrect. For angular momentum to be conserved, the total torque of external forces must be zero ($\sum \vec{M}_{ext} = 0$), not simply their vector sum.

Correct! The vanishing of the vector sum of external forces ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$) alone guarantees the conservation of linear momentum, but not necessarily of angular momentum (e.g., a couple of forces with a non-zero net torque).

questions.topic: Motion of the center of mass
questions.q: If the vector sum of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$), its center of mass moves with uniform rectilinear motion.
questions.hint: Apply the first cardinal equation of dynamics: $M \vec{a}_{CM} = \sum \vec{F}_{ext}$.
explanations: Correct! According to the first cardinal equation of dynamics, if $\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$, the acceleration of the center of mass is zero ($\vec{a}_{CM} = 0$), so it moves with uniform rectilinear motion.
Incorrect. When the sum of external forces is zero, the center of mass maintains a constant velocity (uniform rectilinear motion).

questions.q: If the vector sum of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$), all particles composing the system move with uniform rectilinear motion.
questions.hint: Think about a rigid body in uniform rotation or internal forces between individual particles.
explanations: Incorrect. Individual particles can undergo accelerations due to internal forces within the system or rotational motion.
Correct! Only the center of mass moves with uniform rectilinear motion. Individual particles of the system can rotate, oscillate, or accelerate due to internal forces.

questions.topic: Dynamics of the center of mass
questions.q: If the total torque of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{M}_{ext} = 0$), the center of mass of the system must move with uniform rectilinear motion.
questions.hint: Consider whether zero net torque necessarily implies that the vector sum of forces is also zero.
explanations: Incorrect. The motion of the center of mass is determined by the vector sum of forces ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext}$), not by their torque.
Correct! The torque of forces can be zero even if the net force is non-zero (for example, a single force applied along the line of reference), which would accelerate the center of mass.

questions.q: If the total torque of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{M}_{ext} = 0$), the total angular momentum of the system does not change (it is conserved over time).
questions.hint: Recall the second cardinal equation of dynamics: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{M}_{ext}$.
explanations: Correct! According to the second cardinal equation of dynamics $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{M}_{ext}$, if $\vec{M}_{ext} = 0$, the derivative of angular momentum is zero, so $\vec{L}$ remains constant.
Incorrect. The zeroing of the total torque of external forces is precisely what guarantees the conservation of total angular momentum.

questions.q: If the total torque of the external forces acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{M}_{ext} = 0$), the total kinetic energy of the system is conserved over time.
questions.hint: Think about the work done by internal forces (such as friction, deformation, or internal explosions).
explanations: Incorrect. Kinetic energy can change due to work done by non-conservative internal forces (e.g., inelastic collisions, internal friction).
Correct! The fact that the torque of external forces is zero guarantees the conservation of angular momentum, but kinetic energy can vary due to work done by internal forces.

questions.q: A mass slides, starting from rest, down a frictionless inclined plane that forms an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, located on the surface of a planet where the gravitational acceleration is $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. After traveling $2.5\text{ m}$, what is the speed of the mass (in m/s)?
questions.hint: First calculate the acceleration along the plane ($a = g \sin 30^\circ$), then use the speed formula $v = \sqrt{2 a s}$.
explanations: Correct! $a = 10 \cdot \sin(30^\circ) = 5\text{ m/s}^2$. The speed is $v = \sqrt{2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2.5} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $15\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by forgetting to take the square root when calculating speed.
Incorrect. $10\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by assuming vertical free fall without considering the incline of the plane.
Incorrect. $25\text{ m/s}$ is the value of the squared speed ($v^2$), not $v$.

questions.q: A mass reaches the base of an inclined plane with a speed $v = 5\text{ m/s}$ and continues its motion on a horizontal plane with a dynamic friction coefficient $\mu = 1/2$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). After how many seconds does it stop?
questions.hint: First calculate the deceleration due to friction ($a = \mu g$), then find the stopping time using $t = v / a$.
explanations: Correct! The deceleration due to friction is $a = \mu g = (1/2) \cdot 10 = 5\text{ m/s}^2$. The stopping time is $t = v / a = 5 / 5 = 1\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. $2\text{ s}$ would be obtained by incorrectly considering a halved deceleration of $2.5\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. Calculation error in dividing speed by deceleration.
Incorrect. $5\text{ s}$ corresponds to the initial speed value, not the stopping time.

questions.q: On a planet with gravitational acceleration $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, a girl throws a ball into the air and catches it at the same height $6\text{ seconds}$ later. What was the speed of the ball when it left her hand (in m/s)?
questions.hint: The total time of flight is $t = 6\text{ s}$, so the ascent time is $t_{ascent} = 3\text{ s}$. Use $v_0 = g \cdot t_{ascent}$.
explanations: Correct! The ascent time is half of the total time ($t_{ascent} = 3\text{ s}$). The initial speed is $v_0 = g \cdot t_{ascent} = 10 \cdot 3 = 30\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $60\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained using the total time of $6\text{ s}$ instead of only the ascent time.
Incorrect. $15\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by incorrectly halving the correct speed value.
Incorrect. $10\text{ m/s}$ is the value of gravitational acceleration $g$, not the initial speed.

questions.q: A ball is thrown upward with an initial speed $v_0 = 30\text{ m/s}$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). What maximum height (in meters) does the ball reach relative to the point from which it was thrown?
questions.hint: Use the maximum height formula $h = \frac{v_0^2}{2g}$ or $h = \frac{1}{2}g t_{ascent}^2$.
explanations: Correct! $h = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{30^2}{2 \cdot 10} = \frac{900}{20} = 45\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $6\text{ m}$ is the total flight time expressed in seconds, not height in meters.
Incorrect. $90\text{ m}$ is obtained by omitting the factor of $2$ in the denominator of the maximum height formula ($v_0^2 / g$).
Incorrect. $30\text{ m}$ is the value of the initial speed $v_0$, not the maximum height reached.

questions.q: Two resistors $R_1 = R_2 = 30\ \Omega$ are connected in parallel and connected to a circuit with a voltage source $V = 90\text{ V}$. How much total current (in Amperes) flows through the circuit?
questions.hint: First calculate the equivalent resistance in parallel ($R_{eq} = R/2$), then apply Ohm's law $I = V / R_{eq}$.
explanations: Correct! In parallel, $R_{eq} = 30 / 2 = 15\ \Omega$. By Ohm's law, total current is $I = V / R_{eq} = 90 / 15 = 6\text{ A}$.
Incorrect. $3\text{ A}$ is the current flowing through each individual resistor ($90 / 30$), not the total circuit current.
Incorrect. $1.5\text{ A}$ would be obtained if the two resistors were connected in SERIES ($R_{eq} = 60\ \Omega$).
Incorrect. Error in calculating equivalent resistance or applying Ohm's law.

questions.q: Two $30\ \Omega$ resistors are connected in parallel across a $90\text{ V}$ voltage source. What is the voltage (in Volts) across each resistor?
questions.hint: Recall the fundamental property of voltage in parallel connections.
explanations: Correct! In parallel connections, the voltage across each branch equals the voltage supplied by the generator, i.e., $90\text{ V}$.
Incorrect. $3\text{ V}$ is an incorrect choice and does not correspond to the circuit parameters.
Incorrect. $45\text{ V}$ would be obtained if the two equal resistors were connected in SERIES (voltage divider).
Incorrect. The voltage across parallel components cannot exceed the total generator voltage.

questions.q: A light bulb is connected to a battery that generates a potential difference of $12\text{ V}$. If a current of $0.2\text{ A}$ flows through the bulb, what is the bulb's resistance (in $\Omega$)?
questions.hint: Apply Ohm's first law: $R = \frac{V}{I}$.
explanations: Correct! By Ohm's first law $R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{12}{0.2} = 60\ \Omega$.
Incorrect. $2.4\ \Omega$ is the product $V \cdot I$ (which corresponds to power $P$, not resistance).
Incorrect. $0.0167\ \Omega$ is obtained by mistakenly dividing current by voltage ($I / V$).
Incorrect. Calculation error in dividing by $0.2$.

questions.q: A light bulb connected to $12\text{ V}$ with a current of $0.2\text{ A}$ remains lit for one hour. What is the energy dissipated by Joule heating (in Joules)?
questions.hint: First calculate power $P = V \cdot I$, then multiply by time expressed in seconds ($1\text{ hour} = 3600\text{ s}$).
explanations: Correct! Power is $P = V \cdot I = 12 \cdot 0.2 = 2.4\text{ W}$. Energy is $E = P \cdot t = 2.4 \cdot 3600\text{ s} = 8640\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $144\text{ J}$ is obtained by multiplying power by $60$ (minutes) instead of $3600$ (seconds).
Incorrect. $2.4\text{ J}$ is the power delivered in just one second ($2.4\text{ W}$), not the energy in one hour.
Incorrect. $360\text{ J}$ is a common mistake resulting from dividing $3600$ by resistance or current.
Incorrect. Error in converting the time scale factor.

questions.q: Two resistors $R_1 = 10\ \Omega$ and $R_2 = 20\ \Omega$ are connected in series in a circuit with a $120\text{ V}$ voltage source. How much current flows through the circuit (in Amperes)?
questions.hint: In series, resistances add up ($R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2$). Then apply $I = \frac{V}{R_{eq}}$.
explanations: Correct! Equivalent resistance is $R_{eq} = 10 + 20 = 30\ \Omega$. Total current is $I = \frac{120}{30} = 4\text{ A}$.
Incorrect. $18\text{ A}$ would be obtained by calculating current for a PARALLEL connection ($R_{eq} \approx 6.67\ \Omega$).
Incorrect. $12\text{ A}$ considers only resistor $R_1 = 10\ \Omega$, ignoring $R_2$.
Incorrect. $6\text{ A}$ considers only resistor $R_2 = 20\ \Omega$, ignoring $R_1$.

questions.q: In a series circuit with $R_1 = 10\ \Omega$ and $R_2 = 20\ \Omega$ powered by a $120\text{ V}$ voltage (carrying a current of $4\text{ A}$), what is the voltage across resistor $R_1$ (in Volts)?
questions.hint: Apply Ohm's law to the individual component: $V_1 = I \cdot R_1$.
explanations: Correct! Voltage drop across $R_1$ is $V_1 = I \cdot R_1 = 4\text{ A} \cdot 10\ \Omega = 40\text{ V}$.
Incorrect. $12\text{ V}$ is an arbitrary estimate without analytical basis.
Incorrect. $60\text{ V}$ assumes voltage splits equally in half, which would only be true if resistors were equal.
Incorrect. $80\text{ V}$ is the voltage across the other resistor ($R_2$).

questions.q: In a series circuit with $R_1 = 10\ \Omega$ and $R_2 = 20\ \Omega$ powered by a $120\text{ V}$ voltage (carrying a current of $4\text{ A}$), what is the voltage across resistor $R_2$ (in Volts)?
questions.hint: You can use $V_2 = I \cdot R_2$ or subtract voltage $V_1$ from total voltage $V_{tot}$.
explanations: Correct! $V_2 = I \cdot R_2 = 4\text{ A} \cdot 20\ \Omega = 80\text{ V}$ (or $120\text{ V} - 40\text{ V} = 80\text{ V}$).
Incorrect. $40\text{ V}$ is the voltage across $R_1$.
Incorrect. $60\text{ V}$ would only occur with two equal resistors.
Incorrect. $6\text{ V}$ is a calculation error or misunderstanding of voltage division.

questions.q: Between two parallel conducting wires $1\text{ m}$ long and $0.1\text{ m}$ apart, carrying currents of $10\text{ A}$ in the same direction, what nature of force is generated?
questions.hint: Recall the law of magnetic interaction between currents: do currents in the same direction attract or repel each other?
options: Orthogonal to the line connecting them
explanations: Correct! According to Ampère's law, two parallel conducting wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other.
Incorrect. The force is repulsive only when currents in the two wires flow in opposite directions.
Incorrect. The force is not zero because both currents are non-zero and the wires are at a finite distance.
Incorrect. The force acts along the line joining the two wires (radial direction perpendicular to the wires themselves).

questions.topic: Force between conducting wires - Order of magnitude
questions.q: Two parallel conducting wires $1\text{ m}$ long and $0.1\text{ m}$ apart carry currents of $10\text{ A}$ in the same direction. The order of magnitude of the magnitude of the interaction force is (in N):
questions.hint: Use formula $F = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{I_1 I_2 L}{d}$, with $\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2 \cdot 10^{-7}\text{ N/A}^2$.
explanations: Correct! $F = 2 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \frac{10 \cdot 10 \cdot 1}{0.1} = 2 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 1000 = 2 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ N}$. The order of magnitude is $10^{-4}\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $10^{-2}\text{ N}$ is an incorrect overestimation.
Incorrect. $10^{-7}\text{ N}$ considers only the constant $\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}$, ignoring the contribution of currents and distance.
Incorrect. $10^{-5}\text{ N}$ stems from a calculation error in powers of 10 in the denominator.
Incorrect. $10^{-3}\text{ N}$ would be obtained by improperly rounding up or messing up division by $0.1$.

questions.q: The electric field flux through a closed surface containing a hydrogen atom inside is:
questions.hint: Consider the total net electric charge enclosed within the closed surface and apply Gauss's theorem.
options: Proportional to the charge of the electron
Proportional to the charge of the proton
explanations: Correct! By Gauss's theorem, total electric field flux depends exclusively on enclosed net charge ($Q_{tot} / \epsilon_0$). Since a hydrogen atom is electrically neutral ($Q_{tot} = +e - e = 0$), the flux is zero.
Incorrect. The atom contains both proton and electron; total enclosed charge is zero.
Incorrect. Total net charge inside must be considered, not just positive charge of nucleus.
Incorrect. Flux by Gauss's theorem depends only on internal net charge, not on geometric size of atom or surface.

questions.q: A mass of $10\text{ kg}$ is accelerated vertically upward (with constant acceleration), starting from rest on Earth's surface, until reaching a speed of $10\text{ m/s}$ after $5\text{ seconds}$. How much work is expended to perform this operation (in Joules)? (Use $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.hint: First calculate acceleration ($a = v/t$) and displacement ($h = \frac{1}{2}at^2$). Total work equals change in mechanical energy $\Delta K + \Delta U$.
explanations: Correct! Acceleration is $a = 10/5 = 2\text{ m/s}^2$, height reached is $h = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot 25 = 25\text{ m}$. Work spent is the sum of kinetic energy gained and potential energy: $W = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + m g h = 500\text{ J} + 2450\text{ J} = 2950\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $500\text{ J}$ represents only final kinetic energy ($\frac{1}{2} m v^2$), ignoring work done against gravity to lift mass.
Incorrect. $2450\text{ J}$ represents only gravitational potential energy ($m g h$), ignoring kinetic energy imparted to body.
Incorrect. $490\text{ J}$ is calculation error from incorrect use of kinematic formulas.
Incorrect. $1180\text{ J}$ would be obtained calculating only applied force ($118\text{ N}$) multiplied by time or incorrect height.

questions.q: How many oscillations per second does a mass of $2\text{ kg}$ attached to a spring with spring constant $k = 72\pi^2\text{ N/m}$ make?
questions.hint: Frequency $f$ (oscillations per second) is calculated from angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ using $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}$.
explanations: Correct! Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{72\pi^2}{2}} = \sqrt{36\pi^2} = 6\pi\text{ rad/s}$. Frequency is $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{6\pi}{2\pi} = 3\text{ Hz}$ (3 oscillations per second).
Incorrect. $6$ corresponds to $\omega / \pi$, confusing angular frequency with frequency.
Incorrect. $36$ is obtained by forgetting to take square root of ratio $k/m = 36\pi^2$.
Incorrect. $1/3\text{ s}$ is oscillation period $T = 1/f$, not frequency.

questions.q: Let $B$ be the magnitude of a constant magnetic field, oriented perpendicularly to a circle of radius $r$. The flux of $B$ through the surface of the circle is:
questions.hint: The flux of a uniform magnetic field is $\Phi(B) = B \cdot S \cdot \cos\theta$. Determine circle area $S$ and angle $\theta$.
explanations: Correct! Since field is orthogonal to circle surface, angle with surface normal is $\theta = 0^\circ$ (i.e. $\cos 0^\circ = 1$). Circle area is $S = \pi r^2$, so $\Phi(B) = B \cdot S = \pi r^2 B$.
Incorrect. $2\pi r B$ uses circumference (boundary length) instead of surface area.
Incorrect. There is no factor of $1/2$ in definition of flux for flat surface in uniform field.
Incorrect. Flux would be zero only if magnetic field were parallel to circle surface.

questions.q: A change in magnetic field flux $B$ through the surface enclosed by a circuit:
questions.hint: Recall Faraday-Neumann-Lenz law and principle of energy conservation.
options: induces a current in the circuit, which in turn creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux
induces a current in the circuit, which in turn creates a magnetic field that amplifies the change in flux
produces no effect on current if magnetic field is uniform
causes an electrostatic force that cancels circuit charge
explanations: Correct! By Lenz's law, current induced by change in magnetic flux flows in direction to generate magnetic field opposing change in flux that produced it.
Incorrect. If induced field amplified change, energy would be created from nothing, violating energy conservation principle.
Incorrect. Even if field is uniform, if its flux changes over time, induced current is still produced.
Incorrect. Electromagnetic induction does not cancel electric charge, but sets free charges in conductor into motion.

questions.q: Where is the center of mass of the Earth-Moon system located?
questions.hint: Consider ratio between mass of Earth and Moon (Earth is about 81 times more massive).
options: Inside the Earth (closer to Earth's center)
At exact midpoint of Earth-Moon distance
Outside both Earth and Moon, in empty space
explanations: Correct! Since Earth has mass about 81 times higher than Moon, center of mass is located about $4670\text{ km}$ from Earth's center, inside it (given Earth radius is about $6371\text{ km}$).
Incorrect. Center of mass would be at midpoint only if two bodies had identical mass.
Incorrect. Mass difference is so high center of mass is not in empty space between bodies, but beneath Earth's surface.
Incorrect. Center of mass is always shifted toward body with greater mass.

questions.q: What is the shape of the trajectory described by the center of mass of Earth-Moon system in its revolution around the Sun?
questions.hint: Apply Kepler's first law to center of mass of planetary system.
explanations: Correct! By Kepler's first law, it is the center of mass of entire Earth-Moon system that traverses an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
Incorrect. Although eccentricity of Earth's orbit is small, it is still an ellipse and not a perfect circle.
Incorrect. Parabola corresponds to open escape trajectory, not closed stationary orbit.
Incorrect. Cycloid describes relative motion of single body around center of mass, not motion of center of mass around Sun.

questions.q: What is the approximate time interval between a high tide peak and the next low tide peak at the same location?
questions.hint: Consider that in a lunar day (about 24 hours and 50 minutes) 2 high tides and 2 low tides occur.
explanations: Correct! Full tide cycle includes 2 high and 2 low tides over span of about $24\text{ hours and } 50\text{ minutes}$. Therefore, transition from high tide to next low tide lasts about $6\text{ hours}$ (more precisely ~6 hours and 12 minutes).
Incorrect. $12\text{ hours}$ (about 12 hours 25 minutes) is interval between two consecutive high tides (or two low tides).
Incorrect. $24\text{ hours}$ is roughly duration of full solar day, during which 4 tide phases occur.
Incorrect. $3\text{ hours}$ is too short compared to periodicity of Earth rotation and lunar attraction.

questions.topic: Non-inertial reference frames and apparent weight
questions.q: An elevator starts moving downward with an acceleration $a = \frac{1}{4}g$. What is the apparent weight (in kg) of a $60\text{ kg}$ man while the elevator accelerates?
questions.hint: In a system accelerating downward, fictitious force opposes gravity: $P_{app} = m \left(1 - \frac{a}{g}\right)$.
explanations: Correct! Accelerating downward, normal force exerted by scale is $N = m(g - a) = m\left(g - \frac{1}{4}g\right) = \frac{3}{4}mg$. Apparent mass read is $m_{app} = \frac{3}{4} \cdot 60 = 45\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. $15\text{ kg}$ is obtained calculating only fictitious force $\frac{1}{4}m$ instead of subtracting it from total weight.
Incorrect. $75\text{ kg}$ would be apparent weight if elevator accelerated UPWARD ($1 + 1/4$).
Incorrect. $60\text{ kg}$ is real mass at rest, but during downward acceleration phase one feels lighter.

questions.q: The elevator continues its descent reaching a constant downward speed of $9.8\text{ m/s}$. What is now the apparent weight (in kg) of the $60\text{ kg}$ man?
questions.hint: What is the acceleration of a body moving at constant speed?
explanations: Correct! At constant speed, acceleration is zero ($a = 0$). Consequently, normal force equals real weight force $N = mg$, so apparent weight matches real mass ($60\text{ kg}$).
Incorrect. $4.9\text{ kg}$ is obtained confusing speed value ($9.8\text{ m/s}$) with wrong gravity calculations.
Incorrect. Apparent weight is zero only in absence of gravity or during free fall with acceleration $a = g$.
Incorrect. Constant speed does not double perceived weight.

questions.topic: Non-inertial reference frames and apparent weight
questions.q: The descending elevator decelerates with a deceleration of $\frac{3}{4}g$ until coming to a stop. What is the apparent weight (in kg) of the $60\text{ kg}$ man while elevator decelerates?
questions.hint: Decelerating during downward motion is equivalent to having an upward-directed acceleration vector of magnitude $\frac{3}{4}g$.
explanations: Correct! Downward deceleration corresponds to upward acceleration $a = +\frac{3}{4}g$. Apparent weight becomes $m_{app} = m\left(1 + \frac{3}{4}\right) = 60 \cdot \frac{7}{4} = 105\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. $0\text{ kg}$ would be obtained only in free fall $a = g$ downward.
Incorrect. $15\text{ kg}$ would be obtained taking difference $1 - 3/4$, reversing acceleration direction.
Incorrect. $45\text{ kg}$ was apparent weight during initial downward acceleration phase.

questions.q: A hydraulic lift has two circular pistons of diameter $d_1 = 3\text{ cm}$ and $d_2 = 8\text{ cm}$. What force must be exerted on the smaller piston to allow the larger one to lift a weight of $160\text{ N}$?
questions.hint: Apply Pascal's principle: $\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$. Recall surface area depends on diameter squared ($A \propto d^2$).
explanations: Correct! From $F_1 = F_2 \cdot \frac{A_1}{A_2} = F_2 \cdot \left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^2$, we calculate $F_1 = 160 \cdot \left(\frac{3}{8}\right)^2 = 160 \cdot \frac{9}{64} = 22.5\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $60\text{ N}$ is a frequent mistake resulting from using linear diameter ratio ($160 \cdot \frac{3}{8}$) instead of area ratio (squared diameters).
Incorrect. Error in geometric proportion of surface areas.
Incorrect. Calculation error in squaring fraction.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift with piston diameters $d_1 = 3\text{ cm}$ and $d_2 = 8\text{ cm}$, how far will object on larger piston be lifted if smaller piston is pushed down by $16\text{ cm}$?
questions.hint: Since fluid is incompressible, volume displaced in both branches is same: $V = A_1 \cdot h_1 = A_2 \cdot h_2$.
explanations: Correct! Due to fluid incompressibility, $h_2 = h_1 \cdot \frac{A_1}{A_2} = h_1 \cdot \left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^2 = 16 \cdot \left(\frac{3}{8}\right)^2 = 16 \cdot \frac{9}{64} = 2.25\text{ cm}$.
Incorrect. $6\text{ cm}$ comes from considering linear diameter ratio ($16 \cdot \frac{3}{8}$) instead of ratio squared.
Incorrect. Calculation error in volume proportion.
Incorrect. Error from taking square root instead of squaring proportion.

questions.q: What is the electric field flux through a closed surface due to a charge $Q$ located outside the closed surface?
questions.hint: Recall Gauss's theorem statement regarding charges outside integration surface.
explanations: Correct! By Gauss's theorem, total electric field flux through closed surface is proportional solely to net charge enclosed INSIDE surface ($Q_{int} / \epsilon_0$). An external charge generates field lines entering and leaving surface an equal number of times, making net flux zero.
Incorrect. $\frac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$ would be flux if charge $Q$ were located INSIDE closed surface.
Incorrect. $\frac{2 Q}{\epsilon_0}$ would be flux produced by two charges $Q$ enclosed inside surface.

questions.topic: Gauss's law for magnetic fields (hypothetical monopoles)
questions.q: If magnetic charges (magnetic monopoles) existed, magnetic field flux through a closed surface would be:
questions.hint: Compare with Gauss's theorem for electric field generated by electric charges.
options: proportional to the magnetic charge enclosed within the closed surface
proportional to the electric current passing through the surface
inversely proportional to the area of the closed surface
explanations: Correct! If magnetic monopoles existed, Gauss's law for magnetism would become completely analogous to electrostatics: flux of $\vec{B}$ would be proportional to net magnetic charge enclosed inside closed surface.
Incorrect. Flux is always zero only in real physical reality where isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist and field lines are always closed.
Incorrect. Current passing through surface relates to circulation of $\vec{B}$ (Ampère's law), not flux through closed surface.
Incorrect. By Gauss's theorem, total flux depends solely on internal charges and not on specific surface.

questions.topic: Electric field of a spherical conductor
questions.q: If a homogeneous spherical conductor has a negative charge $Q$, the electric field outside the conductor:
questions.hint: Outside sphere, field is equivalent to point charge located at center of sphere.
options: is directed toward the center of the conducting sphere
decreases when approaching its surface from outside
is zero at all outside points
is tangent to the spherical surface
explanations: Correct! For negative charge $Q$, electric field lines are radial and inward, i.e., directed toward center of conducting sphere.
Incorrect. Approaching surface of sphere ($r$ decreases), field magnitude increases according to $E \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$.
Incorrect. Electric field is zero INSIDE conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, not outside.
Incorrect. In electrostatic equilibrium, electric field on surface and outside is always orthogonal (radial), never tangent.

questions.q: How many Joules of work are required to charge a capacitor of capacitance $C = 0.5\text{ F}$ to a potential difference of $20\text{ V}$ between plates?
questions.hint: Energy (and thus work spent to charge it) is given by $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$.
explanations: Correct! Work required equals stored potential energy: $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0.5 \cdot (20)^2 = 0.25 \cdot 400 = 100\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $200\text{ J}$ is obtained by forgetting factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in formula ($C \cdot V^2$).
Incorrect. $10\text{ J}$ is obtained by simply multiplying capacitance by voltage ($C \cdot V$), which represents charge $Q$, not work.
Incorrect. Calculation error in squaring voltage.
Incorrect. $400\text{ J}$ corresponds to value of $V^2$ alone without considering capacitance.

questions.q: Consider a container containing a liquid up to height $h$. The pressure at bottom of container does NOT depend on:
questions.hint: Recall Stevin's law $P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$ and phenomenon known as 'hydrostatic paradox'.
explanations: Correct! By Stevin's law ($P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$), pressure at bottom depends only on fluid density $\rho$, gravitational acceleration $g$, liquid column height $h$, and surface atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$. Shape or total volume of container does not affect pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
Incorrect. Atmospheric pressure directly affects total bottom pressure by adding to hydrostatic pressure.
Incorrect. Hydrostatic pressure is directly proportional to height $h$ of liquid.
Incorrect. Liquid density $\rho$ is fundamental multiplicative factor of bottom pressure.

questions.q: Suppose you submerge an inverted bucket containing a certain volume $V$ of air at the surface of the sea into the sea. What happens to the volume of air if the inverted bucket is taken to a depth of $40\text{ m}$?
questions.hint: Every $10\text{ m}$ of water depth increases pressure by about $1\text{ atm}$. Apply Boyle's law ($P \cdot V = \text{constant}$).
explanations: Correct! At surface total pressure is $P_1 = 1\text{ atm}$. At $40\text{ m}$ depth water hydrostatic pressure adds $4\text{ atm}$, bringing total pressure to $P_2 = 1 + 4 = 5\text{ atm}$. By Boyle's law ($P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$), volume becomes $V_2 = V/5$.
Incorrect. $V/4$ is typical mistake made considering only hydrostatic pressure of water column ($4\text{ atm}$) and forgetting to add surface atmospheric pressure ($1\text{ atm}$).
Incorrect. $V/3$ would be obtained at depth of only $20\text{ m}$ ($1 + 2 = 3\text{ atm}$).
Incorrect. Air is compressible gas: increasing external pressure, volume decreases inversely.

questions.q: The force exerted by a magnetic field $B$ on a moving charged particle is:
questions.hint: Recall vector definition of Lorentz force: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.
options: orthogonal to both the particle's velocity and the magnetic field $B$
always zero regardless of particle motion
explanations: Correct! From Lorentz force law $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$, vector cross product yields force vector perpendicular (orthogonal) to plane defined by velocity $\vec{v}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$.
Incorrect. If force were parallel to velocity, it would do work and change velocity magnitude (while magnetic force changes only its direction).
Incorrect. Magnetic force is always perpendicular to magnetic field lines.
Incorrect. Force is zero only if particle is at rest ($v = 0$) or moves parallel to magnetic field.

questions.q: Astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) experience weightlessness:
questions.hint: Consider that Space Station and everything inside it are in orbit around Earth.
options: because they are in continuous free fall in Earth's gravitational field
due to the absence of atmosphere in space
because Earth's gravity force at that altitude has become zero
because they are much farther from Earth's center than the surface
explanations: Correct! ISS and astronauts are subject to gravity and are in perpetual orbital free fall (centripetal acceleration coincides with gravitational acceleration). Lack of normal support force creates sensation of weightlessness.
Incorrect. Absence of atmosphere avoids air friction, but does not eliminate gravity force.
Incorrect. At ISS altitude (~400 km), gravitational acceleration is still about 89% of Earth's surface gravity ($g \approx 8.7\text{ m/s}^2$).
Incorrect. Distance would double only at about 6400 km altitude; at 400 km gravity is only slightly reduced.

questions.q: The work done by an ideal gas in an isochoric process (i.e. at constant volume) is:
questions.hint: Recall general formula for thermodynamic work $W = \int P \, dV$.
explanations: Correct! Thermodynamic work requires volume change ($W = P \Delta V$). In an isochoric process volume remains constant (i.e. $\Delta V = 0$), so work done is exactly zero.
Incorrect. Even if pressure changes during isochoric process, without displacement of container walls no work is done.
Incorrect. Temperature change is related to heat exchanged ($Q = n C_v \Delta T$), not work which is zero.
Incorrect. $P \cdot V$ does not represent work in an isochoric process.

questions.q: During an adiabatic compression of an ideal gas, what happens to its temperature?
questions.hint: In adiabatic processes there is no heat exchange ($Q = 0$). Apply first law of thermodynamics $\Delta U = -W$.
explanations: Correct! Since there is no heat exchange with outside ($Q = 0$), work done TO compress gas ($W < 0$) increases its internal energy ($\Delta U = -W > 0$), causing temperature increase.
Incorrect. Temperature would decrease during adiabatic expansion, where gas performs positive work at expense of its internal energy.
Incorrect. Temperature remains constant only in isothermal processes, not adiabatic ones.

questions.q: A wheel rotates with angular velocity $\omega = \pi/5\text{ rad/s}$. How many revolutions does it complete in one minute?
questions.hint: Calculate total angle swept in $60\text{ s}$ ($\theta = \omega \cdot t$) and recall one full revolution equals $2\pi\text{ radians}$.
explanations: Correct! In one minute ($60\text{ s}$) total angle is $\theta = \frac{\pi}{5} \cdot 60 = 12\pi\text{ rad}$. Since $1\text{ revolution} = 2\pi\text{ rad}$, number of revolutions is $N = \frac{12\pi}{2\pi} = 6$.
Incorrect. $12$ is total radians divided by $\pi$, forgetting to divide by $2$.
Incorrect. $3$ would be obtained by incorrectly considering $30\text{-second}$ interval.
Incorrect. $60$ is simply duration in seconds of one minute.

questions.q: What is the equivalent capacitance (in Farads) of a system formed by two capacitors in series with capacitance $C_1 = 2\text{ F}$ and $C_2 = 6\text{ F}$?
questions.hint: For capacitors in series, reciprocals add: $\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$.
explanations: Correct! Equivalent capacitance in series is given by $C_{eq} = \frac{C_1 \cdot C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{2 \cdot 6}{2 + 6} = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5\text{ F}$.
Incorrect. $8\text{ F}$ is direct sum $C_1 + C_2$, which applies to capacitors in PARALLEL, not series.
Incorrect. $4\text{ F}$ is simple arithmetic mean of two values.
Incorrect. Calculation error in inverting sum of reciprocals.

questions.q: A bullet of mass $20\text{ g}$, traveling at a speed of $800\text{ m/s}$, embeds itself in a piece of wood of mass $380\text{ g}$, initially at rest. What will be the speed (in m/s) of the piece of wood (with embedded bullet) immediately after collision?
questions.hint: It is a perfectly inelastic collision. Apply conservation of momentum $m_1 v_1 = (m_1 + m_2) V_{final}$. Remember to convert masses to kg.
explanations: Correct! Converting to kg: $m_1 = 0.02\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 0.38\text{ kg}$. Total final mass $M = 0.02 + 0.38 = 0.40\text{ kg}$. From momentum conservation: $V = \frac{0.02 \cdot 800}{0.40} = \frac{16}{0.40} = 40\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $9.5\text{ m/s}$ stems from calculation error dividing initial speed by incorrect mass ratios.
Incorrect. $42.1\text{ m/s}$ is obtained by dividing momentum by mass of wood alone ($0.38\text{ kg}$), forgetting to add bullet mass.
Incorrect. Calculation error in decimal division.

questions.q: A transformer has $100$ turns in primary circuit and $300$ turns in secondary circuit. If induced potential difference in secondary is $270\text{ V}$, what is potential difference (in Volts) at primary?
questions.hint: Use fundamental transformer equation: $\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{N_1}{N_2}$.
explanations: Correct! Voltage ratio equals turns ratio: $V_1 = V_2 \cdot \frac{N_1}{N_2} = 270 \cdot \frac{100}{300} = \frac{270}{3} = 90\text{ V}$.
Incorrect. $810\text{ V}$ is obtained multiplying by $3$ instead of dividing, mistakenly swapping roles of primary and secondary ($270 \cdot 3$).
Incorrect. $270\text{ V}$ would occur only with $1:1$ turns ratio.
Incorrect. $30\text{ V}$ comes from incorrect scale ratio ($270/9$).

questions.q: An incompressible fluid flows through a pipe of variable cross-section. If its speed in a section of $12\text{ cm}^2$ is $2\text{ m/s}$, what is its speed (in m/s) when area narrows to $3\text{ cm}^2$?
questions.hint: Apply continuity equation for volumetric flow rate: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.
explanations: Correct! By law of continuity $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$, we get $v_2 = \frac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} = \frac{12 \cdot 2}{3} = 8\text{ m/s}$. Speed increases when cross-section decreases.
Incorrect. $0.5\text{ m/s}$ is obtained by reversing proportion ($2 \cdot \frac{3}{12}$), logical error since narrowing pipe speeds up fluid, not slows it down.
Incorrect. $6\text{ m/s}$ comes from incorrect subtraction between areas instead of their ratio.
Incorrect. Calculation error in inverse proportion.

questions.topic: Dynamics of rotating systems - Angular momentum
questions.q: A uniform disk of diameter $2\text{ m}$ has a mass of $10\text{ kg}$. If this disk rotates with an angular velocity of $3\text{ rad/s}$, what is its angular momentum (in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) about its center?
questions.hint: First calculate radius $r = d/2$. Moment of inertia of disk is $I = \frac{1}{2} m r^2$ and angular momentum is $L = I \omega$.
explanations: Correct! Diameter is $2\text{ m}$, so radius is $r = 1\text{ m}$. Moment of inertia of solid disk is $I = \frac{1}{2} m r^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot 1^2 = 5\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Angular momentum is $L = I \omega = 5 \cdot 3 = 15\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.
Incorrect. $25$ is a common error stemming from using diameter value ($2\text{ m}$) instead of radius ($1\text{ m}$) or incorrect moment of inertia calculations.
Incorrect. $30$ would be obtained forgetting factor of $1/2$ in moment of inertia ($m r^2 \omega$).
Incorrect. $7.5$ comes from dividing final result by two again.
